catalog_quote: The underlying contrast is between H and Ø (toneless) since only H tones are active in the tonal rules. There is at most one lexical H tone per morpheme with the exception of Kabwa double H pattern (see below). ... Ikizu also assigns tones to moras but counts syllables. ... None of the languages have underlying contrasts between level H and contour tones, except Ikizu in some restricted contexts. ... In Simbiti and Ikizu, melodic Hs are shifted from the utterance-final syllable to the penult, and in Ikizu, the lexical tone spread does not target the utterance-final syllable. ... new_statements.quote: The underlying contrast is between H and Ø (toneless) since only H tones are active in the tonal rules. There is at most one lexical H tone per morpheme [...] Ikizu also assigns tones to moras but counts syllables. [...] In Simbiti and Ikizu, melodic Hs are shifted from the utterance-final syllable to the penult, and in Ikizu, the lexical tone spread does not target the utterance-final syllable. [...] Ikizu has two tonal patterns for monosyllabic noun stems and three patterns for longer stems (Table 7), with H spreading to the end of the stem. [...] in Ikizu the three underlying patterns are ØØØ, HØØ, and ØHØ. However, Ikizu toneless patterns are realised with a stem-initial H when the noun is pronounced in isolation.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Ikizu is described as a privative-H tone language, not a stress language: noun stems are lexically toneless, penult-H or antepenult-H (Table 7: ùmù-ɾìmì 'farmer' / òmò-ɾámú 'brother-in-law' / ùmú-βísá 'enemy'), with the H spreading rightward to the end of the stem except onto an utterance-final syllable; toneless nouns get a stem-initial H in isolation; the Infinitive H sits on the antepenult of the macrostem. No source opened makes any statement about word stress in Ikizu; the chapter's only 'penultimate stress' remark concerns Zanaki.
new_statements.exceptions: Ikizu allows contour tones 'in some restricted contexts'; the toneless/H contrast of nouns is neutralised in isolation (stem-initial H inserted). Orthography Statement p. 9 adds that phonemic long vowels in noun stems occur almost exclusively in the penult.
new_statements.domain_note: Nominal tone is stated for the stem and for phrase-medial vs utterance-final (isolation) forms; verb melodies are stated for the macrostem. No word-stress domain is discussed.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Ikizu proper (JE402, [ikz]) as spoken in Bunda/Musoma districts; the SIL orthography covers Ikizu-Sizaki jointly (Sizaki [szk] was merged into ikz by ISO change request 2007-033). The Mara chapter's Ikizu data are the same SIL/Helsinki corpus used by Aunio & Robinson.

sources.note: Sec. 2.3 'Tone and syllable structure' (draft pdf p. 7): Mara languages contrast H vs toneless; Ikizu assigns tones to moras but counts syllables; utterance-final melodic H shifts to the penult and lexical H spread does not target the utterance-final syllable. Nominal tone (draft p. 9, Table 7): Ikizu nouns have three underlying patterns ØØØ / HØØ / ØHØ, i.e. toneless, penult H, antepenult H, with H spreading to the end of the stem; toneless nouns surface with a stem-initial H in isolation. sources.note: Sec. 2.3 Tone, p. 19: 'Ikizu has lexical tone on nouns, but this tone does not have a high functional load and therefore is not written in the orthography.. Ikizu also has a variety of grammatical tone melodies, but none of them are contrastive.' Sec. 2.1.2, p. 9: in noun stems phonemic long vowels occur 'almost exclusively in the penultimate syllable'. No stress or accent statement.

sources.citation: Aunio, Lotta. 2015. A typological perspective on Bantu nominal tone: the case of Ikoma-Nata-Isenye in western Tanzania. Southern African Linguistics and Applied Language Studies 33(3): 359-371. doi:10.2989/16073614.2015.1105106 [Helda accepted manuscript]
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Draft pdf p. 12 (print c. p. 368), one paragraph on Ikizu: aligns nominal lexical tones to the right edge of the stem; nouns are toneless (umu-ɾimi 'farmer') or have penult H (omo-ɾámu) or antepenult H (umú-βisa); systematic rightward H spread except utterance-finally; toneless utterances not allowed, so toneless nouns get an antepenultimate or stem-initial H in isolation; phrase-medially [-Oblig(H)] [-Culm(H)]. No stress statement.
